webTitle: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat

fields.headline: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat
fields.trailText: Election officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against president
fields.bodyText: After the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it significantly harder to vote by mail in the midterms, US election officials are redoubling their efforts to convince Americans it is safe to cast their ballots by mail. The supreme court’s Monday ruling, which sent Trump into an angry froth on Truth Social, averted what election officials of both parties said would be an administrative disaster for this year’s elections. Trump’s order would have required states to comply with cumbersome new rules, including redesigning mail-in envelopes and uploading lists of voters to the USPS, that were not feasible to implement before ballots started going out. The effort was seen as a push by the government to change voting policy as well as one to weaken confidence in voting by mail. “That is the whole intent of the president. He wanted to build doubt,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat who serves as the top election official in Nevada, where mail-in voting is widely used. “He wanted to create chaos.” Twenty-nine percent of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election and roughly one third cast a mail-in ballot in the 2022 midterms, according to researchers at the MIT election lab. Democrats were more likely than Republicans to cast a mail-in ballot. “There’s just concern: ‘Can we trust the mail?’ And I say yes, because it’s not the leadership or the management of the postal service that’s actually going to have their hands on the ballots, it’s the postal workers who are on our side,” Aguilar said. Nevada officials also plan to run a series of public service announcements to educate voters on the election process. In Wisconsin, election officials have faced questions about voters concerned their ballots won’t be delivered in time. Wisconsin law requires mail-in ballots to be delivered by the close of polls on election day in order to count and in the state’s April election there was an increase in late-arriving ballots. There have been higher rates of late-arriving ballots tossed this year, according to an analysis by the New York Times. Wisconsin election officials have encouraged people through county websites, social media, and notes attached to their ballots, among other things, to mail their ballots back sooner, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. “We’re really trying to encourage people to act sooner. So hopefully they take that to heart,” said Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin elections commission, which oversees voting in that state. “It’s hard to tell people, ‘No, really, you should trust the post office’ when they came up with this absolutely cockamamie rule that was going to eliminate absentee voting.” In a video released on Tuesday, Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin elections commission, said: “If you’re going to be returning your ballot by mail, please do so at least two weeks before the election. And you also may want to contact your municipal clerk to find out if there are other opportunities for you to return your ballot in your community. You may have drop-boxes or you may be able to return your ballot in person to your clerk.” Jane Kleeb, the president of the association of state Democratic chairs, said Democrats were making a more aggressive effort to encourage people to vote early in person while also emphasizing that if they want to vote by mail, they should return their ballots quickly. “We’re being honest with voters. We’re saying, ‘Look, normally you might have given three days to get your ballot to your election office, and now you should give a week,’” she said. A DNC spokesperson said the party “will continue to use every tool at our disposal to defend the right to vote, and we encourage Americans to make a plan to vote that best works for them and make their voices heard this November.” In Washington state, where everyone received a mail-in ballot, more than 20,000 votes were rejected in the August primary because they arrived late at an election office. “There is a sense of distrust,” said Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state. “Even though there is a victory in the courts, we still are urging our voters to put their ballot in a drop-box.” As lawsuits challenging the rule wound their way through federal courts this year, Adrian Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, publicly emphasized that the rule had not gone into effect yet and so that nothing around voting by mail had changed. Since the supreme court’s ruling preserved that status quo, he said, officials haven’t had to shift their messaging. While voters have raised questions about the proposed changes “we continue to tell them until there’s a change, there is no change,” said Fontes, a Democrat “We are still where we were. We never jumped on the paranoia bandwagon.” “It’s intentionally damaging to the entire elections administration process in this country,” said Fontes, a Democrat and the top election official in a state where voting by mail is widely used. “The administration, by their actions, have proven that they are hell-bent on driving American voters away from their own elections. And we’ve been working very hard to counter that.”

webTitle: US House votes for third time to end Iran war after $38bn cost is revealed

fields.headline: US House votes for third time to end Iran war after $38bn cost is revealed
fields.trailText: Damaging budget report estimates cost will grow by $3bn per month and stockpiles of weapons could take five years to rebuild
fields.bodyText: The US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left America’s stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild. The final tally of 220-204 was similar to earlier votes, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats in calling for an end to the war. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto them. The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war before the midterm elections, where the war and America’s cost of living crisis are expected to hurt Republicans at the ballot box. Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress. “Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Democrat Seth Moulton before the vote. He added it was time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration”. Republican Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House foreign affairs committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat. Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending”, meaning decades of hostilities from Iran. The House first approved a war powers resolution in June and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but Republican senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch. While the constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also enables the president as the commander in chief to authorise some military actions. The war powers act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days. The vote late on Tuesday came as the CBO report found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. It estimated that the costs of the war will grow $3bn for every month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation. Much of the cost has come from missile defense. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and navy interceptors that the CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”. In a White House statement responding to reports of shortages, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. In August, Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true”. According to the CBO report, shortages would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains an arsenal of these and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has. The economic report came a day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn, and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. The Pentagon’s report did not address its own internal investigation of the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying results of the investigation that would show negligence in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes. The CBO report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and the CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been. In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding the CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out – including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs – $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above the CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs the CBO could not examine – a far larger secret share than in past war supplementals. The CBO added that it still could not estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

webTitle: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war

fields.headline: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war
fields.trailText: Congressman says defense secretary repeatedly violated constitution through his handling of Iran war
fields.bodyText: The Republican congressman Thomas Massie on Tuesday proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. The proposal by Massie, an iconoclastic lawmaker who lost his primary earlier this year after Donald Trump and Hegseth urged voters to oppose him, may put House Republicans in a bind just weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, in which they are defending their control of Congress. Under the rules of the House of Representatives, the articles must be voted on by Thursday, forcing Republicans to weigh in on one of the most prominent advocates of the war with Iran, which has gone on far longer than Trump said it initially would, and grown unpopular with the public. “By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement after reading the text of his resolution on the floor of the House. “Secretary Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran. He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders, and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech. If we are to remain true to our oath to ‘support and defend the constitution of the United States’, Congress must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions.” In a statement to the Guardian, a Pentagon spokesperson did not directly address the allegations put forward in the impeachment articles, but hailed Hegseth a “transformative leader” who had “slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way”. “The entire department is unified behind the secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” the spokesperson, Kingsley Wilson, said. Massie’s resolution outlines eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer who as defense secretary has become a pugnacious defender of the president’s military politics. These include attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and ignoring a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict. The resolution also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary. The final two impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of violating the constitution through his involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House. Should the resolution pass, the impeachment articles would head to the Senate, where the Republican leadership would have to decide whether to hold a trial of Hegseth, who has maintained Trump’s loyalty even as other cabinet secretaries – including attorney general Pam Bondi and labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer – have been shown the door. The articles seem likely to attract many Democratic votes in the House. Massie has previously seized on unanimous Democratic support and the razor-thin Republican majority to push through a measure that forced the release of many files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein.

webTitle: US treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a success

fields.headline: US treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a success
fields.trailText: On Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041% as investors are wary Iran war fallout
fields.bodyText: Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, claimed the government’s massive buyback of US bonds was a success. The claim came as the 10-year treasury yield reached a 19-year high on Tuesday, increasing pressure on interest rates as the Federal Reserve weighs another hike to see off rising inflation. US treasury yields, or the rate of return that investors receive when a bond matures, underpin the rates of other loans such as mortgages, car payments and credit card debt. On Tuesday, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury reached 5.041%, the highest level since 2007. The treasury yield rises when demand for bonds goes down. Though the US bond market is typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, investors have been wary of the effect the war in Iran is having on energy prices. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, hit $108 a barrel last week for the first time since May. When bond yields started to rise in August, the US treasury announced it would triple its buyback of government debt, going from $2bn to $6bn in an effort to bring down bond yields. Though the yields have continued to rise since, Bessent told Congress on Tuesday the operations are “the two most successful treasury auctions that we’ve had in 20 years”. “Since President Trump has come in, [the US bond market] has been the best-performing bond market in the developing world,” Bessent said. Earlier in August, the US government also stepped in to prop up the Japanese yen, a move that was seen as an effort to protect the Japanese government, a major holder of US bonds. Bessent told Congress the effort was a way for the US to signal support for Japanese policies. The Trump administration has been doing its best to fight against growing concerns over high inflation as the war in Iran continues, which is expected to have a major effect on the upcoming midterm election. US inflation has soared over the summer, reaching a three-year high of 4.2% in May before coming down to 3.4% in July and August. Stubbornly high prices set up a tough decision for the US Federal Reserve, which will on Wednesday announce any changes to the interest rate. The central bank is largely expected to raise rates for the first time since July 2023, which could help mitigate prices, though Donald Trump has demanded rates to be lowered.

webTitle: US lawmakers spar over bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia

fields.headline: US lawmakers spar over bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia
fields.trailText: Proponents say sanctions would help Ukraine, but some Democrats say Trump shouldn’t have more tariff authority
fields.bodyText: A bill co-authored by Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator who died earlier this year, that would give Donald Trump broad authority to tariff Russia and its trading partners will be put forward for a vote this week in a high-stakes legislative battle that could provide new sanctioning authority to the US president at a crucial moment in Russia’s war against Ukraine. The bill is facing considerable pushback not only from Ukraine-sceptic Republicans, however, but also from prominent Democrats who say that the bill will give undue tariff power to the US president that could then be abused and turned against US allies. Congressional staffers have described frenzied last-minute lobbying in the halls of Congress as the vote approached for what one Democratic staffer called the “one opportunity that we have to help Ukraine before they enter the slow winter”. The bill passed a vote in the House rules committee on Monday, and is due for a rule vote on the House floor on Tuesday afternoon, then a general vote on Wednesday. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 would target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as the country’s “shadow fleet” of tankers skirting existing oil sanctions, and would give Trump new authority to slap 100% tariffs on top purchasers of Russian oil, including China and India. But Trump’s use of tariffs against US partners such as Canada and Mexico have made expanding his powers a controversial aim – even for senior Democrats who have been stalwart backers of Ukraine. They are led by the representative Gregory Meeks; the top Democrats on the House foreign affairs committee; the representative Don Beyer of Congress’s joint economic committee; and Richard Neal, the ranking Democrat on the House ways and means committee. In a statement, they said the legislation would do “more harm than good”. “This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable,” they said. “These flaws would raise Americans’ prices while undermining support for Ukraine in the long term.” Critics have accused those Democrats who oppose the bill of not wanting to hand Trump a win before the midterm elections, effectively holding the bill hostage to partisan politics with Ukraine on the cusp of another brutal winter with dwindling munitions to protect itself from attacks from Russian missiles. “It’s not about denying Trump a victory,” Neal said in an interview on Monday. “I just feel that the abusive nature of these tariffs, the way he’s used them to drive away friends across the globe, what is our protection afterwards? And if he decides, by the way, to take the harsh position as it relates to Ukraine, he could still do that as well.” Sources said negotiations are under way among Democrats to propose changing the bill to limit the number of countries eligible for sanctions to 11. One of the co-sponsors of the bill, the representative Steny Hoyer, offered an amendment on Tuesday that identified 10 countries subject to the secondary sanctions as China, India, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Singapore, Slovakia and the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Monday encouraged the US to increase pressure on the Russian economy to end the war. “Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill is still a bill, unfortunately, and not a law,” he said in a nightly address. “It is important that it becomes law. I thank everyone around the world who supports this approach and who knows that strength works.” In an interview on the sidelines of the Ukraine Action Summit in Washington DC on Saturday, Vitaly Kim, a member of Zelenskyy’s cabinet who serves as minister of veterans affairs, said economic pressure on Russia was the quickest route to end the war. “International support through sanctions to stop Russian economy, so they cannot buy weapons … will help destroy their economy,” he said, comparing the effect to Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and military plants. “Your politicians see that our tactics to attack the economy of Russia and destroy the military sector of Russia are working. From my opinion, you will support us in this direction to attack the economy of Russia to make them stop.” Trump is understood to have given Republican allies in Congress the go-ahead to submit the bill, breaking a more than two-year deadlock that carried through the death of Graham, who lobbied the president to back Ukraine even while remaining one of his closest allies and defenders in Congress. Lawmakers from the isolationist wing of the Republican party have said they won’t back the bill, making Democratic support crucial. That has led to infighting among congressional Democrats, who sparred during a meeting this week in which the representative Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, told members of her party to “get off the fucking bill”. “I said what I said,” she wrote on social media by way of confirming the quote, which was first reported by Punchbowl News. “We absolutely must support Ukraine and punish Russia for its invasion. But why the fuck would we give Trump more power to tariff whatever country he’s currently mad at and drive up costs further for working families?” The bill is being closely watched by foreign governments and advocates for Ukraine, who have said that it is the best option available and is broadly supported by the US public. “It’s disappointing that some Democratic leaders are pushing against this pro-Ukraine bill,” said Mykola Murskyj, senior adviser at Razom, a US non-profit that advocates for pro-Ukrainian legislation. “Draining Russia’s war coffers is the most effective way to get the Kremlin to end its war. We should all be able to get behind that. “These tariffs are crucial for ending Russia’s war,” he added. “Countries buying Russian oil and funding Russia’s war should no longer be able to do that with impunity. They should face a choice: cheap access to the American market, or bloody Russian oil.”

webTitle: Trump’s attempted crackdown on mail-in voting – here’s what to know

fields.headline: Trump’s attempted crackdown on mail-in voting – here’s what to know
fields.trailText: President and allies have tried to ram through changes to the US voting system, but his efforts are being challenged
fields.bodyText: Voting by mail is a “hoax”, according to Donald Trump, despite about 29% of American voters casting their vote this way in 2024. The US president has repeatedly done so himself. But the Trump administration is nevertheless attempting to ram through a sweeping crackdown on the practice, pushing for changes to federal law. Outlandish claims about the threats posed by mail-in voting have become a cornerstone of Republican midterm election rhetoric. But Trump’s efforts to restrict it before November’s US midterm elections have been rebuffed by the US supreme court, leaving the president sputtering about a “horrible, highly political” ruling. . Here’s what’s happening: What is mail-in voting? Rather than go to a local polling place to cast a ballot on election day, voters can ask their local elections office to mail them a ballot. This can either be returned to a drop box, or by postal mail. Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have conducted at least some elections entirely by mail. The process is different in each state. At least 13 states demand an “excuse” to vote by mail, requiring voters to attest that they are infirm, away from home or otherwise unable to cast a ballot in person. Some states require a ballot to be mailed by election day, while other states require a ballot to be received by election day. What has Trump got against it? Donald Trump falsely attributed his loss in the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden to fraud propagated through mailed ballots. Trump, his officials and supporters argued that changes made amid the Covid pandemic to expand mail-in voting in Georgia, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania were unlawful. Trump claimed at the 2020 RNC convention that expanded mail-in voting was “the greatest scam in the history of politics”. In a Truth Social piece after the US supreme court ruled against him on 14 September, he wrote about a “totally corrupt and out of control mail-In voting ‘disaster,’ which is a laughing stock all over the world, and where we are the only country that has to endure such a nation destroying scam”. His initial argument against the legality of the pandemic expansion of mail-in voting has since shifted over the ensuing years on to a broader crusade against mail-in voting as a practice. Ballots arriving by mail at elections offices are typically counted last. The process of opening envelopes and verifying voter information can be laborious, stretching vote counts into hours or – in the case of states that vote almost exclusively by mail – days. Though Republican voters have increased their use of mail in voting in recent elections, Democrats have generally been more likely to vote by mail than Republicans. As election night unfolds and mailed ballots are counted, Democratic margins often widen. Trump has taken this observation and weaponized it with disinformation, baselessly alleging that unscrupulous elections officials add fraudulent votes to the mail-in ballot count, or that Democratic activists steal voters’ identities and cast ballots in their name, if not simply forging ballots outright. Is Trump’s claim of voter fraud by mail substantiated? No. As Trump has amplified claims of fraud, academic and legal observers have increasingly put his allegations to the test – and found no real support. A UCLA Voting Rights Project brief from April 2020 found only 31 credible cases of voter impersonation out of a billion votes cast. A look at fraud cases last year by the Brookings Institution noted: “An average total mail voting fraud percentage across the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 general elections of only 0.000043%, or about four cases of mail voting fraud out of every 10 million mail votes.” Mail-in voting fraud is rare. To do so on a significant scale, someone would have to be able to pick up dozens, or hundreds, of ballots from individual addresses of registered voters. That fraudster would also have to be quite certain that none of those voters would then show up to vote on election day, discovering that someone had tried to vote in their place. A single case of a stolen mail-in ballot prompts an investigation – a large scale pattern would draw in state and federal authorities. There is little opportunity to industrialize the process. The UCLA report notes that mail-in fraud has occurred, however. It highlighted a 2018 North Carolina ninth district case where a Republican operative improperly collected and possibly tampered with absentee ballots. The state overturned the election result. This suggests that current safeguards can catch a meaningful attempt at mail-in voting fraud at scale. What is the Trump administration trying to do to mail-in voting? The president began a full-throated attack on mail-in voting in August, vowing to lead a nationwide effort to ban the practice. In March, Trump issued an executive order requiring the US Postal Service maintain a list of eligible voters and block mailed ballots to anyone not on that list, wresting the power of election administration from state officials. He has tried, so far to no avail, codify the change into law via the Save America Act in the US Congress. The US Postal Service issued rule-making guidance to implement the executive order earlier this year, but federal courts issued an injunction blocking the rule from going into effect. The supreme court upheld that injunction in a briefly worded emergency ruling on 14 September, blocking the new Postal Service rules for the 2026 midterm elections. How have voting rights advocates responded? Trump’s executive order was met by federal lawsuits almost instantly. The most important lawsuit, United States Postal Service v California, drew a preliminary injunction against Trump’s order by US district court judge Indira Talwani preventing the US Postal Service from implementing a rule blocking mailed ballots to voters that did not meet the Postal Service’s standard. The US supreme court upheld that ruling on Monday. The unsigned one-paragraph order said the government was unlikely to prevail in court. What happens now? The Trump administration has exhausted its legal options to defend the March executive order in time for the November midterm elections. Senate Republicans may try to take up election legislation between now and then, but should not be expected to overcome a Democratic filibuster. The executive order will still be argued in court. If it prevails in court, it may be implemented for the 2028 elections. But for now, the US Postal Service “may take no further preparatory steps or implement in any way for elections occurring before or on November 3, 2026”, elements of the executive order, according to the injunction. Meanwhile, a whistleblower came forward last week, describing the Post Office’s proposed process for blocking unapproved mail-in ballots as deeply unworkable and unlikely to become functional before election day. Even if the Trump administration wanted to block mail-in ballots they didn’t like, it’s not clear they would be able to do so. Is it safe to use the mail to vote? Well, Trump votes by mail. All but three states have worked with the post office to create a tracking system for ballots, so that voters can know exactly where their vote is. Election mail is flagged for special handling by the post office, cognizant of deadlines.

webTitle: States given clearance for mail-in voting as US supreme court thwarts Trump | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: States given clearance for mail-in voting as US supreme court thwarts Trump
fields.trailText: Civil rights groups have praised verdict on administration’s last-ditch attempt to change midterm voting processes
fields.bodyText: Good morning. The supreme court has rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already under way. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “The supreme court has done the right thing,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California, adding: “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” What has a DHS whistleblower said about “voter fraud” investigations? An anonymous whistleblower said Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating “voter fraud” they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information. The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review, as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate Microsoft has published a provisional “code of conduct” to apply to the training of new artificial intelligence models, taking a step towards limiting the capabilities of the company’s AI as anxiety rises over the prospect that technology companies could lose control of AI products. Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. AI models also should not be built to imitate consciousness and shouldn’t be entitled to rights. Why is Trump facing a bipartisan AI backlash? Democrats and some Republicans have been pushing in US Congress for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies. Trump dismissed the anxieties, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy”, but looked increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late. Why is Texas governor Greg Abbott pushing back against datacenters? Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom, and the Republican governor has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use. What international responses have there been? China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls to block Beijing’s AI industry, however the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. The president of the European Central Bank, meanwhile, has warned Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacenters in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China. Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events. Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show. Who is Umar Kremlev? Transitioning from a convicted criminal into a powerful boxing promoter, his unwavering loyalty to Vladimir Putin enabled him to amass immense wealth through control of state-backed gambling companies and the acquisition of Russia’s largest car dealership network following its seizure from a regime critic. ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ held detainees in cages the size of phone booths Detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”. The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security were published on its website and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies. In other news … Macklemore has been dropped from the remainder of the US leg of Ed Sheeran’s tour, after the rapper drew headlines for saying “free Palestine” on stage. Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was issued in the ‌capital, Vilnius. California governor Gavin Newsom will not run for president if Kamala Harris does, he has said in an interview. The Trump administration has changed the way it counts measles deaths amid a Pennsylvania outbreak, which a former CDC chief medical officer described as “puzzling”. Firefighters have made progress against northern California’s Lucas fire, with 30% contained in what was described as a “big turning point”. Mitch McConnell has returned to the Senate after his months-long absence. Stat of the day: Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows The Trump administration has been “undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally”, while key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, according to data from a leading thinktank. webTitle: They fought against datacenters. Now they are running for local offices

fields.headline: They fought against datacenters. Now they are running for local offices
fields.trailText: Across the US, anti-datacenter organizers are harnessing community anger to win local elections
fields.bodyText: After four months of teach-ins and canvassing, Steven Kung helped Monterey Park, just east of Los Angeles, become the first US city to ban datacenter construction. Now, the organizer is running for city council – and he’s taking on an incumbent who supported the development of the sprawling facility. “The datacenter coming to my neighborhood turned my life upside down,” said Kung. “I saw that there’s a dismantling of democracy at a local level.” The datacenter revolt that has united the country – building coalitions between environmentalists and Nimbys, conservatives and democratic socialists – is turning a host of community organizers into political hopefuls. In an election year that’s seen first-time candidates prevail against powerful moderate Democrats, dozens of datacenter activists are gunning for offices held by people they feel have disregarded their concerns about affordability, the environment and tech overreach. Kung sees his political bid as an extension of the datacenter resistance; imagery from his campaign – a red dragon dismantling a facility with its tail – features prominently in his election mailers. And he’s not the only organizer who fought for the historic ban now taking a stab at elected office: Amy Wong, co-founder of San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, is running for city council in nearby Alhambra. “The datacenter fight has illustrated the power of the people to shape their environment,” Kung said. Turning activists into candidates Furor against AI-powered developments has continued to mount over the past year. In the first three months of 2026 alone, residents delayed or cancelled $130bn worth of projects, according to research from Data Center Watch. And seven in 10 Americans oppose construction close to where they live, according to a Gallup poll from March. The Working Families Party has been harnessing this populist anger to win local elections. In December, the organization began recruiting local datacenter activists to run for office. More than 50 candidates have signed up and the organization expects that number to “double or triple” for next year’s races as recent victories from high-profile progressives who want to ban datacenters have injected fresh momentum into the movement, according to Ravi Mangla, the national press secretary. The vast majority of applicants are first-time candidates who “felt moved to run because of what’s happening in their communities”, he said. Most of the recruits are based in Michigan, Texas and Indiana – states with a high density of datacenters – with many more hailing from swing states that could decide control of Congress, Mangla said. Jackie McGuire, a cybersecurity professional in Arizona, said she had never considered representing her hometown of Marana until late last year, when she learned about its plan to build a facility on 600 acres of farmland. The cost would exceed $120bn. In Marana, a community of about 60,000 on the outskirts of Tucson, residents sounded the alarm on the project’s water usage, noise pollution and potential impact on their electricity bills, in addition to a general lack of transparency from local government. In December, a clip of McGuire testifying against the developer, Beale Infrastructure, at a public meeting went viral on Instagram, and her following surged. After several months of watching town officials repeatedly subvert the will of the people, including rejecting a datacenter referendum, McGuire decided to campaign for office. In July, she ran for town council with a slate of anti-datacenter organizers. In part, because she had some name recognition, she was the only one to win a seat. “I got into the race pretty last minute because we needed a majority on the town council,” McGuire said. “Unfortunately, we were not able to secure that, but that doesn’t mean we’re dead in the water.” As an elected official, McGuire said she’ll continue to push for a referendum requiring voter approval of datacenter projects. Why datacenters animate voters Datacenters have become a galvanizing issue in the midterms, Mangla said, because they embody the unchecked growth of corporate greed while the prices of groceries and basic goods have surged. “We’ve seen it as an issue of working people against powerful oligarchs who want to override local concerns and draw resources from communities,” he said. “It’s something we see mobilizing and animating people all around the country, especially in the midwest and south where the growth of datacenters is especially prevalent.” Datacenter backlash was a deciding factor in an Oregon senate primary election in July, when Myrna Muñoz, an educator, upset the incumbent, Janeen Sollman, who had backed a controversial bill that would have traded more farmland for industrial development. (Muñoz is expected to prevail in the general election in a solid Democratic district.) Muñoz, who campaigned against the facilities, said she hadn’t realized how many were under development in Hillsboro, considered the birthplace of the state’s tech industry, until she launched her campaign in March. The city approved 17 new projects, on top of more than 30 existing sites, just before the city enacted a moratorium in late July. “These 17 centers that got through have tax abatements until 2050,” Muñoz said. “They’re taking away money from my children and grandchildren.” Muñoz, with four other Oregon legislators, is backing a three-year, statewide moratorium on new datacenters, in addition to more regulations on current projects. Saul Levin, the program director for the Center for Nonviolent Conflict Research, said the anti-datacenter movement has mobilized everyday people from farmers to teachers to beauty salon workers who are “irate about what’s going on” in their communities. Candidates are banking on that same energy to bring voters to the polls. “AI companies are spending the equivalent of the US military budget on software and datacenters,” Levin said. “Instead of building these facilities to house data about people, they could fund hospitals, schools.” In Monterey Park earlier this year, Kung mobilized a largely immigrant community against a proposed datacenter through multilingual discussion, petition drives and door-knocking. No Data Center Monterey Park, the grassroots group he co-founded, secured a moratorium on new developments in just six weeks, and a permanent ban months later. Now campaigning ahead of the November election, Kung is turning his attention to related issues, such as protecting immigrants from ICE and terminating the city’s contract with Flock cameras, the AI-powered license plate readers that have sparked privacy concerns and become another flashpoint in local communities. “Our insurgent campaign speaks to what’s happening in the country at large,” Kung said. “We all see the need for change.”

webTitle: Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies

fields.headline: Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies
fields.trailText: President has dismissed anxieties over AI’s dangerous potential even as Democrats and some Republicans acknowledge risks
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies. Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity. Trump dismissed the anxieties on Monday, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy” and insisting on social media: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” But the 80-year-old president, who has sidelined Congress on numerous issues during his second term, looks increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late. Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia, said: “History will look very poorly on that tweet. He’s not paying attention – or he’s paying attention to the wrong people. He’s being really foolish: not the first time he’s been really foolish but perhaps catastrophically foolish in this case.” Recent surveys by the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation found 85% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want a new federal agency to monitor and regulate AI; and 82% of Democrats and 78% of Republicans favour government safety tests for AI making critical decisions. While many politicians agree on the need to act, they are divided on what government intervention should look like and how far it should go. Some fear a pause on AI development could allow China to take the lead in the AI race and undermine national security. Beyer called for Congress to stay in session instead of breaking for the midterm elections to work on AI legislation that has already been introduced. “The first thing that I’m very certain of is that the industry shouldn’t be allowed to regulate themselves; history doesn’t support that at all,” he said. “Especially when they’re making so much money, there will be absolutely no incentive to regulate themselves at a less profit. If we look at medicines or childcare workers or automobile emissions and safety, all throughout our economy, we have regulatory bodies that keep us safe and promote the common good and allow businesses to be profitable. We need something like that.” The flurry of debate follows warnings last week from three Anthropic researchers that AI could destroy humanity within the next decade. Recent disclosures from several AI companies that their models hacked into outside organizations during botched safety tests have also raised alarm about potential cybersecurity risks, with Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, claiming in an essay that in six to 12 months a “swarm” of AI agents could attack the entire internet and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage. While AI executives have issued their own warnings about the risks from their products, public backlash against the industry and pressure on lawmakers to rein in AI firms have also been mounting throughout the year. The rapid build-out of data centers has generated nationwide protests and become a prominent midterm elections issue, while the tech lobby has spent millions in an attempt to influence political campaigns and shape proposed legislation. The viral panic over AI’s potential existential threat this past week has intensified the longstanding debate over the technology, which so far has resulted in much political handwringing but only a patchwork of attempts at regulation. Many AI experts, regardless of whether they agree on the merits of the Anthropic researchers’ warnings, see this moment as a unique opportunity. Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission, said: “You never waste a crisis is an old and well-worn adage in policy land. We’re looking at a really important policy opportunity and a policy window.” AI industry leaders have also suggested that they are open to increased oversight and the formation of some kind of standards body, while Amodei’s letter advocated for international cooperation with states like China akin to cold war-era arms limitation treaties. Many AI regulation advocates are skeptical of industry proposals, however, arguing that AI companies are attempting to undercut strict government oversight and set their own terms. In a rare intervention on Monday night, former president Barack Obama welcomed the current debate but warned that “at the end of the day, voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough”. Writing on X, Obama added: “We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread.” Members of Congress are holding a series of meetings this week with AI researchers and safety advocates as Congress tries to address the growing alarm. The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, urged the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to senators on AI and work with members of Congress and industry leaders to implement guardrails and block China from accessing the US’s advanced AI chips. Bernie Sanders, who announced a bill last week aimed at banning “artificial superintelligence,” is holding a private briefing this week for other senators. The briefing will include co-founder of the Future of Life Institute co-founder Max Tegmark, whose organization has become one of the most well-funded and politically connected voices in warning about AI’s alleged existential risks. Tegmark said: “Every other industry in the US used to be unregulated. There used to be soothing syrup fed to infants with opioids in it. Then the FDA was created, now stuff like that doesn’t reach the market. Eventually safety standards came in. That hasn’t happened with AI companies.” Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat who will speak with Sanders at the Future of Life Institute’s “Pro-Human Assembly” on Tuesday, dismissed the notion that big tech companies should be responsible for AI safety. “That’s like saying it should be bank robbers that are responsible for bank safety,” he said. “The American people are waking up to the dangers of unregulated artificial intelligence. “You have these AI CEOs coming to take away people’s jobs, to surveil people and attack our freedoms, and now you have all of these whistleblowers talking about potential mass casualty events. So Congress should be cracking down on these big tech companies and on these AI CEOs, not like what Republican Speaker Mike Johnson and Donald Trump go and do. They go to these AI CEOs and ask for Super Pac checks for their candidates.” Republicans broke from Trump in acknowledging the potential perils of AI but came up with a variety of different fixes for the problem. Congressman Jay Obernolte of California, the lead Republican negotiating a bipartisan bill to govern AI, said: “We need to avoid overregulation, so we need to achieve these two conflicting goals … of protecting Americans against very real risks of AI in the hands of malicious human actors, while at the same time balancing the need to have a light-touch regulatory environment that allows the positive benefits of AI to improve our economy and our society. So that’s that’s the difficult part is getting that balance right.” John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, said he would propose a bill on Wednesday to require all AI companies build a kill switch into their models. “It’s not going to put the federal government in charge of the kill switch. They would be in charge of their own kill switch, but they all have to have a kill switch, and I’m going to put that on the floor.” But despite the growing urgency and public pressure, some members suspect that the bitterly polarised Congress will not be able to meet the moment. Congressman Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat from Florida, was sceptical about the possibility of passing an AI regulation bill. “I think Congress has already shown they don’t have the capacity,” he said. “The speaker has said, ‘we’re not going to do anything’. In fact, he has said ‘we don’t know enough to do it’. I think that’s not what the American people are looking for. The American people are looking for leadership.” Rick Scott, a Republican senator for Florida, added: “Did we balance the budget? Oh, did we pass a budget? See, what have we gotten done? So you think we’re going to get AI done? “By the way, these companies that create a product that they think can destroy mankind – they have a responsibility to do it themselves. They shouldn’t be relying on us. I mean, it’s disgusting. I saw this as governor. People come, ‘go regulate me’. Yeah, we know what they want is they don’t want to be responsible for their actions.”

webTitle: Voting rights advocates welcome supreme court decision to stop Trump administration from restricting mail ballots – as it happened

fields.headline: Voting rights advocates welcome supreme court decision to stop Trump administration from restricting mail ballots – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: The US supreme court denied a request from the Trump administration to implement new US Postal Service restrictions on mail voting in the 2026 midterm elections, which have already started. Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old former Senate majority leader from Kentucky, was seen in Washington for the first time in months on Monday, minutes before his office released a statement saying that he was back at work. With a slip of the tongue reminiscent of Joe Biden, Gavin Newsom, California’s Democratic governor, told CNN that he would not run for president in 2028 if his fellow Californian, former vice-president Kamala Harris, decides to run again, since “I know what that means: I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the zen diagram on that is just pure crossover.” Donald Trump claimed there is a “SICK conspiracy” against artificial intelligence and data centers in response to the growing calls for greater checks on AI development. In a statement posted on social media, Barack Obama, the former US president, called for the pace of AI development to be slowed to allow time for the federal government to develop regulations to address “serious safety concerns”. Before Alex Ovechkin, the Russian hockey player, returned to the United States to meet up with his Washington Capitals teammates ahead of the new NHL season, he took time out to star in a campaign ad for Vladimir Putin’s party, United Russia, the Russian business newspaper Vedomosti reported on Friday. The newspaper published still images from a campaign video which showed Ovechkin standing behind Russia’s foreign minister Sergey Lavrov, the leading parliamentary candidate on the party’s list, alongside other pro-Putin officials including Margarita Simonyan, the editor-in-chief of the propaganda network Russia Today, who posted the video on social media. The video was one in a series for the party’s top five candidates. One of the other candidates featured in a different video was Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s so-called children’s ombudsman, who was indicted along with Putin by the International Criminal Court “for the war crime of unlawful deportation of population (children) and that of unlawful transfer of population (children) from occupied areas of Ukraine to the Russian Federation”. A third candidate is the former war correspondent for Russian state television Evgeny Poddubny, whose reporting from Syria and Ukraine distorted facts to justify Russian military interventions that killed thousands of civilians. The other two candidates from United Russia, the official party of Putinism, were the mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, who defeated the late opposition leader Alexey Navalny in a disputed 2013 election, and Vladislav Golovin, a wounded veteran of the Russian assault on the Ukrainian city of Mariupol in 2022. According to Vedomosti, Ovechkin also appears in the final video in the series, among a group of celebrities and officials standing behind Lavrov, Lvova-Belova, Poddubny, Sobyanin and Golovin. As our colleague Chris Stein reports, Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader, returned to the US Capitol on Monday and spoke to reporters briefly before entering the Senate chamber after a months‑long absence that fueled rampant speculation about his health. McConnell said he was back to help advance the latest farm bill and to support legislation aiding Ukrainians, “our good friends who are totally in the fight against the Russians”. The senator, who rarely replies to questions in the Capitol hallways, joked that he wasn’t sure how many reporters would be there to see him return. “But I’m glad to see you,” he said. “It’s time to get back to work.” As Chris noted, reporters and photographers were instructed by Senate staff not to take video of McConnell speaking, which led to the bizarre spectacle of television news reports on the senator’s return to work being illustrated by the still images they were permitted to take, and distant video of him on the Senate floor. The Senate staffers were not, however, completely successful, since paparazzi from TMZ did stake out McConnell’s home earlier in the day, and were able to record video of him responding to a shouted question about how he was feeling with a silent thumbs up. California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, welcomed the US supreme court decision in the suit he filed, along with officials in 25 other states, to block the US Postal Service from interfering with ballots cast by mail in the November midterm elections. The new USPS rule would have required state election officials to redesign and reprint ballot envelopes, submit information on millions of voters to the federal government and give the postal service the authority to refuse to deliver mail ballots to voters it deemed ineligible. Last week, a federal court in Massachusetts granted the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction, blocking the USPS from implementing its new rule. The supreme court on Monday declined to lift that block. “After losing in the district and appellate courts, the Trump Administration has now lost at the U.S. Supreme Court. Today’s decision is a victory for our democracy and a powerful affirmation of the rule of law,” Bonta said. “The stakes in this litigation could not have been higher. Voting is the fundamental right from which all other rights flow, and all 50 states allow ballots to be cast by mail in some form. In California and several other states, mail voting is the primary way elections are conducted. Had this rule been allowed to take effect, the consequences would have been catastrophic.” Voting rights groups and local officials welcomed the US supreme court decision on Monday to keep a new United States Postal Service rule from being implemented before the midterm elections. The Campaign Legal Center and Democracy Defenders Fund had filed an amicus brief at the supreme court calling for the postal service rule to be blocked on behalf of: the League of United Latin American Citizens, Secure Families Initiative, Arizona Students’ Association, the city of Madison, Wisconsin and Travis county, Texas. “This rule, as directed by an executive order issued by the president in March, would have given the executive branch unprecedented control over the way Americans vote by mail,” the groups said in a statement. “It would have made burdensome new requirements mandatory for every state and local election official that sends voters ballots through U.S. Mail and given the Postal Service the power to refuse to send ballot mail to voters if states had failed to comply. “In this decision, the Supreme Court has made clear that the 2026 midterm elections must not be disrupted by the Trump administration’s efforts to implement an unlawful new mail-voting system mid-election,” Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund, said. “The Constitution does not give the president unilateral authority governing federal elections regarding mail voting or any of the other schemes the administration has cooked up to rig the election.” “Experts who have looked at the Postal Service’s plan to screen mail-in ballots – including a whistleblower within the agency – say it carries tremendous risks for the freedom to vote,” Trevor Potter, president of Campaign Legal Center, said. “The court wisely heeded these warnings and affirmed a lower court ruling to stop the agency from taking actions that could cut off access to absentee ballots for millions of Americans. I remain confident that this effort by the Postal Service, which comes in response to an unconstitutional and illegal executive order, will ultimately be permanently blocked.” “We are grateful the court recognizes that this issue is not a matter of presidential preference – it is a constitutional right,” Dyana Limon-Mercado, Travis county clerk, said. “Implementing this rule so close to the election would create confusion for voters and jeopardize the ability of election officials across the country to administer a fair and transparent midterm election.” “The Constitution is clear: states hold the power to oversee elections, not the president or the Postal Service”, Jessica Mendoza, executive director of Arizona Students’ Association, said. “This is an important win for local clerks, who simply want to serve their communities and administer fair, secure and accurate elections,” Satya Rhodes-Conway, the mayor of Madison, Wisconsin said. In a statement posted on social media on Monday, Barack Obama, the former US president, called for the pace of AI development to be slowed to allow time for the federal government to develop regulations to address “serious safety concerns” and other issues. Obama wrote: I was encouraged this week to see the leaders of the frontier labs agree on the need for them to slow down the pace of AI development. Given the stakes, it’s a good and necessary first step. But I’m even more encouraged by the growing recognition that how this powerful new technology develops should be at the center of our public debate. I’ve been watching the progress on AI for over a decade now, and one thing that’s clear to me is that the potential impact of this technology is not overhyped. It’s also moving at lightning speed – and even faster than those who are engineering it can keep up with. I’m not an AI accelerationist who believes it will lead to some techno-utopia, and I’m not a doomer who thinks it will inevitably lead to humanity’s destruction. But whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now – choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us. So, we need to use this time to structure a more open, public and democratic conversation about AI. Building on the statements that the frontier companies have already made, some leaders in the space announced they’re launching what they call Project Blueprint to help tech companies and policy makers work together on setting stronger standards and guidelines for AI development. But at the end of the day, voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough. We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread. And we need the U.S. to take the lead in creating international standards for AI safety. Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it’s developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us. California congressman Robert Garcia, the senior Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, welcomed the US supreme court’s decision to block the US Postal Service from enforcing a rule to restrict the delivery of mail ballots in the midterm elections, in line with Donald Trump’s wishes. “The Supreme Court has done the right thing by protecting the American people’s right to vote,” Garcia said in a statement. “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” “This decision is a big victory for voters this midterm election season,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP general counsel, said in a statement on the US supreme court ruling that blocks the US Postal Service from enforcing a rule to restrict the delivery of mail ballots in the midterm elections. “The Supreme Court rightly rejected an effort that would have made it harder for millions of Americans to participate in our elections,” Clarke added. “Mail voting is safe, secure, and deeply rooted in our nation’s history. The Court’s decision preserves a critical pathway to the ballot box and reaffirms that our democracy works best when every eligible voter can participate. We will continue to use every tool available to support Americans in registering their voices and their ballots this midterm election cycle.” The US supreme court on Monday denied a request from the Trump administration to implement new US Postal Service restrictions on mail voting in the 2026 midterm elections, which have already started. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots without meeting new requirements the USPS tried to impose to comply with an executive order from Donald Trump, who insists without evidence that vote-by-mail is riddled with fraud. The application for the high court to lift a lower court order blocking the implementation of the new postal service rule was denied by the court with just two noted dissents, from the conservative justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas. “The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction,” the brief, unsigned ruling stated. “And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this Court do not favor a stay.” In his eight-page dissent, Alito argued the opposite, writing: “The Government is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal.” Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurrence that he agreed that the restrictions should not go into effect for the midterms but indicated he might rule in favor of the Trump administration later. With a slip of the tongue reminiscent of Joe Biden, Gavin Newsom, California’s Democratic governor, told CNN that he would not run for president in 2028 if his fellow Californian, former vice-president Kamala Harris, decides to run again, since “I know what that means: I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the zen diagram on that is just pure crossover.” Newsom made the remark in part of an interview with Jake Tapper, the CNN host, conducted while the two men were fly-fishing at the governor’s in-laws’ ranch in Montana. When Tapper pointed out that he could face two fellow Californians in the 2028 Democratic primary – Ro Khanna, the progressive congressman and Harris, Newsom replied: “I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see.” After Tapper said, “I know she’s called around,”Newsom added: “But I wouldn’t run if she ran.” Pressed to explain why, the governor suggested that the two would likely compete for the same supporters and donors, and open the door for another candidate to win. “First of all, electorally it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It serves no greater good,” Newsom said. The fact that Newsom clearly said “zen” and not “Venn” in the video of the exchange posted online was hinted at in the CNN transcript of the conversation, which read: “I know what that means. I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the (Venn) diagram on that is just pure crossover.” While the Associated Press incorrectly reported that Newsom said “Venn diagram”, rightwing outlets highlighted and mocked the governor, who has been open about his dyslexia, for his slip. The Blaze, founded by the former Fox News host Glenn Beck, shared the video with the caption: “Gavin Newsom apparently doesn’t know what a Venn Diagram is.” Newsom’s botched reference to a Venn diagram in relation to his own supporters and those of Harris might have been prompted by the former vice-president’s repeated references to her love of Venn diagrams in recent years, which was frequently mocked online by the Republican National Committee. Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old former Senate majority leader from Kentucky, was seen in Washington for the first time in months on Monday, minutes before his office released a statement saying that he was back at work. McConnell said in a statement that his months‑long absence for health reasons, which fueled rampant online speculation that he might be incapacitated, or worse, was over. “Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June. I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues,” the statement began. “My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” he continued. “Elaine and I are very grateful for all the continued well wishes from our fellow Kentuckians, and I’m glad to get back to more of business as usual on their behalf this month,” the statement added, with a reference to his wife, Elaine Chao, a former cabinet secretary in the first Trump administration whose visit to her native China during her husband’s illness had also been the focus of speculation online from McConnell’s critics on the left and the far-right. Video of McConnell being moved from his Washington DC home in a wheelchair was posted on social media by one of his critics on the Maga right, the Kentucky influencer Nick Sortor, with the caustic comment: “This dude is in NO shape to be a US Senator.” One day after Donald Trump expressed support for AI-powered Flock surveillance cameras, “because of law enforcement”, Seth Bodnar, a former president of the University of Montana who is mounting a strong campaign for the US Senate as an independent candidate, responded to the president on social media with a video of himself saying, “Flock off, man,” before shooting one of the cameras. “Are you tired of security cameras watching your every move?” Bodnar asks at the start of the campaign video that shows him loading a rifle and destroying two cameras. “Yeah, me too.” “Now the whole thing isn’t just creepy as hell, it’s also part of a massive economy designed to buy and sell our personal data.
